prompt: Summarize the excerpt from 'dmoi3-tablet' (chunk 22.2) about mathematics: In this case, when both P → Q and Q → P are true, we say that P and Q are equivalent and write P ↔ Q . This is the bicon
true_answer: In this case, when both P → Q and Q → P are true, we say that P and Q are equivalent and write P ↔ Q . This is the biconditional we mentioned earlier. If and only if. P ↔ Q is logically equivalent to ( P → Q )∧( Q → P ) . Example: Given an integer n , it is true that n is even if and only if n 2 is even. That is, if n is even, then n 2 is even, as well as the converse: if n 2 is even, then n is even. You can think of “if and only if” statements as having two parts: an implication and its converse. We might say one is the “if” part, and the other is the “only if” part.
